pepper_bacterial_spot.label: Pepper — Bacterial Spot
pepper_bacterial_spot.description: A bacterial disease caused by Xanthomonas species that produces small, dark, water-soaked spots on leaves and fruit, common in warm, humid, or rainy conditions.
symptoms: Small, dark brown to black spots with yellow halos on leaves
Raised, scab-like spots on fruit
Leaves may yellow and drop in heavy infections
Spots often start on lower, older leaves
pepper_bacterial_spot.cause: Bacteria in the genus Xanthomonas, spread in warm, wet weather.
pepper_bacterial_spot.spread: Splashing rain or overhead irrigation, contaminated seed or transplants, and handling wet plants.
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed and transplants
Avoid overhead watering; water at the base
Rotate away from peppers and tomatoes for 2+ years
Avoid working with plants while foliage is wet

organic: Apply copper-based bactericide preventively before wet periods
Remove and destroy infected leaves and fruit
Improve airflow through spacing and pruning
chemical: Copper + mancozeb combination products, applied on a 7-10 day schedule
Rotate products to slow copper resistance in bacterial populations
preventive: Start with certified disease-free seed
Avoid overhead irrigation
Sanitize tools and hands between plants
Rotate crops away from solanaceous plants

pepper_healthy.label: Pepper — Healthy
pepper_healthy.description: No signs of disease detected. Leaf color, texture, and structure appear normal.
symptoms: Uniform green color
No spotting or lesions
Firm, unblemished leaf tissue
prevention: Continue routine monitoring
Maintain consistent watering at the base
Keep good spacing and airflow

organic: No treatment needed — keep monitoring weekly
chemical: No treatment needed
preventive: Rotate crops each season
Scout weekly for early symptoms

potato_early_blight.label: Potato — Early Blight
potato_early_blight.description: A fungal disease caused by Alternaria solani producing dark, target-shaped concentric rings, typically starting on older, lower leaves.
symptoms: Brown to black spots with concentric target-like rings
Yellowing tissue around each lesion
Lower leaves affected first, progressing upward
Can also cause dark, sunken lesions on tubers
potato_early_blight.cause: Fungus Alternaria solani, surviving in soil and infected plant debris.
potato_early_blight.spread: Wind-blown spores, splashing rain or irrigation, and contaminated tools.
prevention: Rotate crops on a 2-3 year cycle
Hill soil around plants to protect developing tubers
Water at the base and avoid wetting foliage
Remove volunteer potato plants

organic: Remove and destroy infected lower leaves promptly
Apply copper-based fungicide at first sign of spots
Mulch to reduce soil splash onto foliage
chemical: Chlorothalonil or mancozeb, applied every 7-10 days
Alternate fungicide classes to reduce resistance risk
preventive: Use certified seed potatoes
Rotate away from solanaceous crops
Destroy plant debris after harvest

potato_late_blight.label: Potato — Late Blight
potato_late_blight.description: An aggressive water-mold disease caused by Phytophthora infestans, capable of destroying a field within days in cool, wet weather. Historically responsible for the Irish potato famine.
symptoms: Large, irregular, water-soaked grey-green blotches
White fuzzy mold on the underside of leaves in humid conditions
Rapid browning and collapse of leaf tissue
Reddish-brown dry rot inside affected tubers
potato_late_blight.cause: Oomycete pathogen Phytophthora infestans, favored by cool temperatures and prolonged leaf wetness.
potato_late_blight.spread: Airborne spores traveling long distances in cool, damp, overcast weather; also spreads through infected seed tubers.
prevention: Plant certified, disease-free seed potatoes
Choose resistant varieties where available
Avoid working in wet fields
Monitor regional late blight forecasts during wet seasons

organic: Remove and destroy infected plants immediately, do not compost
Apply copper-based fungicide preventively before wet weather
Increase spacing and staking for airflow
chemical: Chlorothalonil or mancozeb applied preventively
Systemic fungicides containing mefenoxam for active outbreaks
Rotate chemical classes to avoid resistance build-up
preventive: Use certified seed potatoes only
Avoid overhead watering, especially in the evening
Destroy cull piles and volunteer plants
Scout fields daily during cool, humid spells

potato_healthy.label: Potato — Healthy
potato_healthy.description: No signs of disease detected. Leaf color, texture, and structure appear normal.
symptoms: Uniform green color
No spotting or wilting
Firm, intact leaf structure
prevention: Continue routine monitoring
Maintain consistent watering and balanced fertilization
Hill soil to protect developing tubers

organic: No treatment needed — keep monitoring weekly
chemical: No treatment needed
preventive: Rotate crops each season
Scout the field weekly

tomato_bacterial_spot.label: Tomato — Bacterial Spot
tomato_bacterial_spot.description: A bacterial disease caused by Xanthomonas species producing small, dark, water-soaked spots on leaves, stems, and fruit, common in warm, wet conditions.
symptoms: Small, angular, dark brown to black leaf spots with yellow halos
Raised, scabby spots on green fruit
Leaf yellowing and drop in severe cases
tomato_bacterial_spot.cause: Bacteria in the genus Xanthomonas, favored by warm, wet weather.
tomato_bacterial_spot.spread: Splashing rain, overhead irrigation, contaminated seed or transplants, and handling wet foliage.
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed and transplants
Avoid overhead watering
Rotate away from tomatoes and peppers for 2+ years
Avoid handling wet plants

organic: Apply copper-based bactericide preventively
Remove and destroy infected leaves and fruit
Space and stake plants for airflow
chemical: Copper + mancozeb combination products every 7-10 days
Rotate active ingredients to slow resistance
preventive: Start with certified disease-free seed
Avoid overhead irrigation
Sanitize tools between plants
Rotate crop families

tomato_early_blight.label: Tomato — Early Blight
tomato_early_blight.description: A fungal disease caused by Alternaria solani that produces dark, target-shaped concentric rings on older, lower leaves first, gradually moving upward through the canopy.
symptoms: Brown to black spots with concentric rings, resembling a target
Yellowing tissue surrounding each spot
Lower, older leaves affected first
Leaves eventually wither, dry out, and drop
tomato_early_blight.cause: Fungus Alternaria solani, which survives in soil and plant debris between seasons.
tomato_early_blight.spread: Wind-blown spores, splashing rain or irrigation water, and contaminated tools or hands.
prevention: Rotate crops on a 2-3 year cycle away from solanaceous plants
Space plants for good airflow
Water at the base, avoid wetting foliage
Mulch to prevent soil splash onto lower leaves

organic: Prune and destroy infected lower leaves promptly
Apply neem oil spray every 7 days as a preventive barrier
Use a copper-based organic fungicide at first sign of spots
Improve airflow by staking and pruning dense growth
chemical: Chlorothalonil-based fungicide, applied every 7-10 days
Mancozeb, alternated with a different mode of action to reduce resistance
Always follow label rates and pre-harvest intervals
preventive: Rotate crop families each season
Use certified disease-free seed or transplants
Avoid overhead irrigation; water early in the day
Remove and destroy plant debris after harvest

tomato_late_blight.label: Tomato — Late Blight
tomato_late_blight.description: An aggressive water-mold disease caused by Phytophthora infestans, capable of destroying an entire field within days under cool, wet conditions. Historically responsible for the Irish potato famine.
symptoms: Large, irregular, water-soaked grey-green blotches
White fuzzy mold on the underside of leaves in humid conditions
Rapid browning and collapse of leaf tissue
Dark, greasy-looking lesions on stems and fruit
tomato_late_blight.cause: Oomycete pathogen Phytophthora infestans, favored by cool temperatures and prolonged leaf wetness.
tomato_late_blight.spread: Spreads extremely fast through airborne spores over long distances, especially in cool, damp, overcast weather.
prevention: Plant resistant varieties where available
Avoid working in wet fields to limit spore transfer
Destroy volunteer potato and tomato plants
Monitor local blight forecasts during wet seasons

organic: Remove and bag infected plants immediately, do not compost
Apply copper-based fungicide preventively before wet weather
Increase plant spacing and stake for airflow
chemical: Chlorothalonil or mancozeb applied preventively before an outbreak
Systemic fungicides containing mefenoxam for active infections
Rotate chemical classes to avoid resistance build-up
preventive: Choose resistant cultivars
Avoid overhead watering, especially in the evening
Scout fields daily during cool, humid weather
Destroy infected material far from the growing area

tomato_leaf_mold.label: Tomato — Leaf Mold
tomato_leaf_mold.description: A fungal disease caused by Passalora fulva (formerly Fulvia fulva) that thrives in humid, poorly ventilated environments such as greenhouses and tunnels.
symptoms: Pale green to yellow patches on upper leaf surfaces
Olive-green to grey velvety mold on the leaf underside
Leaves curl, wither, and drop in severe cases
Rarely affects fruit directly
tomato_leaf_mold.cause: Fungus Passalora fulva, favored by high humidity (above 85%) and limited air circulation.
tomato_leaf_mold.spread: Spores spread through air currents, water splash, and contact with contaminated tools or clothing.
prevention: Ventilate greenhouses and tunnels to reduce humidity
Avoid overhead watering and wetting foliage late in the day
Space and prune plants for airflow
Use resistant tomato varieties where available

organic: Increase ventilation and reduce humidity below 85%
Remove and destroy affected leaves
Apply a sulfur or copper-based organic fungicide
chemical: Chlorothalonil-based fungicide labeled for leaf mold
Apply at the first sign of yellow patches, repeat per label
preventive: Use fans or vents to keep humidity in check
Water early in the day so foliage dries quickly
Avoid dense planting in enclosed structures

tomato_septoria_leaf_spot.label: Tomato — Septoria Leaf Spot
tomato_septoria_leaf_spot.description: A fungal disease caused by Septoria lycopersici that produces many small, circular spots with dark borders and light centers, usually starting on lower leaves.
symptoms: Numerous small, circular spots with dark brown margins and tan-grey centers
Tiny black specks (fruiting bodies) visible in the center of older spots
Lower leaves affected first, yellowing and dropping progressively
Rarely affects fruit
tomato_septoria_leaf_spot.cause: Fungus Septoria lycopersici, which overwinters in plant debris and soil.
tomato_septoria_leaf_spot.spread: Splashing water, wind-driven rain, and contact with contaminated tools or hands.
prevention: Mulch around plants to reduce soil splash
Water at the base, avoid overhead irrigation
Remove lower leaves that touch the soil
Rotate crops away from tomatoes for at least a year

organic: Remove and destroy infected lower leaves as soon as spotted
Apply copper-based fungicide at first sign of spots
Mulch heavily to block spore splash from soil
chemical: Chlorothalonil or mancozeb, applied every 7-10 days during wet periods
Continue applications through the growing season if conditions stay humid
preventive: Clean up and destroy plant debris after harvest
Stake and prune for airflow
Avoid working with wet plants

tomato_spider_mites.label: Tomato — Spider Mites (Two-Spotted)
tomato_spider_mites.description: A pest infestation, not a fungal or bacterial disease, caused by the two-spotted spider mite (Tetranychus urticae). Thrives in hot, dry conditions and can rapidly weaken plants by feeding on leaf tissue.
symptoms: Fine yellow or white stippling/speckling on leaves
Leaves take on a bronzed or dusty appearance
Fine webbing on the underside of leaves and between stems in heavy infestations
Leaves may curl, dry out, and drop
tomato_spider_mites.cause: Two-spotted spider mite (Tetranychus urticae), a tiny arachnid pest that thrives in hot, dry, dusty conditions.
tomato_spider_mites.spread: Wind, contact with infested plants or tools, and movement between closely spaced plants.
prevention: Keep plants adequately watered — drought-stressed plants are more susceptible
Avoid excess dust around plants (hose down pathways in dry weather)
Encourage natural predators like predatory mites and ladybugs
Inspect new plants closely before introducing them

organic: Spray leaves (especially undersides) with a strong jet of water to dislodge mites
Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil, covering leaf undersides thoroughly
Introduce predatory mites (e.g. Phytoseiulus persimilis) for biological control
chemical: Miticide labeled for two-spotted spider mite (not a standard fungicide)
Rotate miticide classes — mites build resistance quickly
Avoid broad-spectrum insecticides that also kill natural predators
preventive: Maintain consistent irrigation, especially in hot weather
Reduce dust near plantings
Monitor undersides of leaves weekly during hot, dry spells

tomato_target_spot.label: Tomato — Target Spot
tomato_target_spot.description: A fungal disease caused by Corynespora cassiicola producing brown lesions with concentric rings, similar in appearance to early blight but caused by a different pathogen.
symptoms: Circular brown lesions with faint concentric rings
Lesions can merge into larger irregular blighted areas
Can affect leaves, stems, and fruit
Fruit lesions appear sunken with a pitted texture
tomato_target_spot.cause: Fungus Corynespora cassiicola, favored by warm temperatures and high humidity.
tomato_target_spot.spread: Wind-blown spores, splashing water, and contaminated tools or hands.
prevention: Rotate crops away from tomatoes for at least a year
Space and stake plants for airflow
Avoid overhead watering
Remove and destroy crop debris after harvest

organic: Remove and destroy infected leaves and fruit promptly
Apply copper-based fungicide at first sign of lesions
Improve airflow through pruning and spacing
chemical: Chlorothalonil or azoxystrobin-based fungicide, applied per label interval
Rotate fungicide classes to limit resistance
preventive: Practice crop rotation
Avoid dense planting
Water at the base early in the day

tomato_yellow_leaf_curl_virus.label: Tomato — Yellow Leaf Curl Virus
tomato_yellow_leaf_curl_virus.description: A viral disease (TYLCV) transmitted by whiteflies, causing severe stunting, leaf curling, and yield loss. There is no cure once a plant is infected — management focuses on prevention and vector control.
symptoms: Upward curling and yellowing of leaf margins
Stunted, bushy plant growth
Reduced flowering and fruit set
Smaller, thickened leaves
tomato_yellow_leaf_curl_virus.cause: Tomato yellow leaf curl virus (TYLCV), transmitted exclusively by the whitefly Bemisia tabaci.
tomato_yellow_leaf_curl_virus.spread: Whiteflies feeding on infected plants and moving to healthy ones; virus is not spread by seed or mechanical contact.
prevention: Plant resistant or tolerant tomato varieties where available
Use insect netting or reflective mulch to deter whiteflies
Remove and destroy infected plants immediately to reduce virus source
Control weeds that can host whiteflies nearby

organic: There is no cure for the virus itself — remove and destroy infected plants
Use yellow sticky traps and insecticidal soap to reduce whitefly populations
Introduce whitefly predators/parasitoids where feasible
chemical: Insecticide targeted at whiteflies (the vector), not the virus itself
Rotate insecticide classes to avoid whitefly resistance
Time applications to seedling and early growth stages when plants are most vulnerable
preventive: Start with certified virus-free transplants
Use physical barriers (row covers, screens) during establishment
Remove volunteer tomato plants and nearby weed hosts
Monitor and control whitefly populations season-long

tomato_mosaic_virus.label: Tomato — Mosaic Virus
tomato_mosaic_virus.description: A viral disease (ToMV, closely related to TMV) causing mottled, distorted foliage and reduced yield. Highly stable and easily spread mechanically — there is no chemical cure.
symptoms: Mottled light and dark green mosaic pattern on leaves
Leaf distortion, curling, or fern-like narrowing
Stunted plant growth
Fruit may show internal browning or uneven ripening
tomato_mosaic_virus.cause: Tomato mosaic virus (ToMV) or the closely related Tobacco mosaic virus (TMV).
tomato_mosaic_virus.spread: Highly contagious through mechanical contact — hands, tools, clothing — and can persist in soil and plant debris for a long time; also spread via infected seed.
prevention: Use certified virus-free seed
Wash hands and disinfect tools between handling plants
Avoid using tobacco products before handling plants (TMV can transfer from tobacco)
Remove and destroy infected plants immediately

organic: There is no cure for the virus itself — remove and destroy infected plants
Disinfect tools with a diluted bleach or milk solution between uses
Avoid working in the garden when foliage is wet to limit mechanical spread
chemical: No chemical treatment cures a viral infection
Focus chemical use on secondary pest control if applicable
preventive: Start with certified virus-free seed and transplants
Practice strict hand and tool hygiene
Rotate crops and remove plant debris after harvest
Avoid smoking or handling tobacco near plants before working with them

tomato_healthy.description: No signs of disease detected. Leaf color, texture, and structure appear normal.
symptoms: Uniform green color
No spotting, curling, or discoloration
Firm, intact leaf structure
prevention: Continue routine monitoring for early signs of stress or disease
Maintain consistent watering and balanced fertilization
Keep good airflow and spacing between plants

organic: No treatment needed — keep monitoring weekly
chemical: No treatment needed
preventive: Rotate crops each season
Water at the base early in the day
Scout the field weekly for early symptoms
